subject: English
topic: Active and passive voice II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'Ravi is writing a letter.'

options.option_text: A letter is written by Ravi.
A letter is being written by Ravi.
A letter was written by Ravi.
A letter has been written by Ravi.

questions.explanation: Present continuous active — 'is + V-ing' → present continuous passive — 'is/are + being + V-3'. Subject 'Ravi' moves to the agent slot ('by Ravi'); object 'a letter' becomes the new subject. Option A uses simple present passive (wrong tense). Option C uses past passive. Option D uses present perfect passive.

questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'The students must complete the assignment.'

options.option_text: The assignment is completed by the students.
The assignment must be completed by the students.
The assignment must have been completed by the students.
The assignment will be completed by the students.

questions.explanation: With modals (must, can, may, should, would, could, might) active → passive: modal + BE + V-3. 'Must complete' → 'must be completed'. Option C (must have been completed) converts a past modal perfect, not 'must complete'. Option D wrongly changes the modal. Perfect modal passive: 'must have been completed' = active 'must have completed'.

questions.stem: Change to active voice: 'Hindi is spoken in India by most people.'

options.option_text: India speaks Hindi.
Most people in India speak Hindi.
People speak Hindi India.
Hindi speaks most people.

questions.explanation: Passive 'is spoken by most people' → active 'most people speak'. Keep location phrase ('in India') where it fits most naturally. Option A drops the subject ('most people') — changes meaning. Option D inverts the subject and object, which is nonsense here.

questions.topic: Active and passive voice II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'Who wrote this poem?'

options.option_text: Who was this poem written by?
By whom was this poem written?
Whom wrote this poem?
By who is this poem written?

questions.explanation: For Wh-questions with 'who' as subject in the active → 'by whom' (object pronoun) in the passive. Subject (who) wrote → object. Form: 'By whom + auxiliary + subject + V-3?'. Active past simple 'wrote' → passive past simple 'was written'. Option A is colloquially acceptable but examiners prefer 'by whom'. 'Whom wrote' and 'by who' are ungrammatical.

questions.topic: Active and passive voice II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'Open the door.'

options.option_text: The door is opened.
Let the door be opened.
The door was opened.
Open should be the door.

questions.explanation: Imperatives in the passive — 'Let + object + be + V-3'. 'Please open the door' → 'Let the door be opened, please' / 'You are requested to open the door.' 'Do not disturb' → 'Let the door not be disturbed.' Option A is a declarative statement, not an imperative.

questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'The teacher has explained the lesson.'

options.option_text: The lesson was explained by the teacher.
The lesson has been explained by the teacher.
The lesson is explained by the teacher.
The lesson had been explained by the teacher.

questions.explanation: Present perfect active 'has/have + V-3' → present perfect passive 'has/have + been + V-3'. 'Has explained' → 'has been explained'. Option A — simple past. Option D — past perfect ('had been explained' = 'had explained'). Option C — simple present passive.

questions.stem: Change to passive: 'They were building a house.'

options.option_text: A house was built by them.
A house was being built by them.
A house is built by them.
A house has been built by them.

questions.explanation: Past continuous active 'was/were + V-ing' → past continuous passive 'was/were + being + V-3'. 'Were building' → 'was being built' (new subject 'a house' is singular). Option A converts to simple past, changing the tense sense. Option D — present perfect. Option C — simple present.

questions.stem: Select the correct passive voice form of: 'The government will launch a new welfare scheme next month.'

options.option_text: A new welfare scheme will be launched by the government next month.
A new welfare scheme will be being launched by the government next month.
A new welfare scheme will have been launched by the government next month.
A new welfare scheme is launched by the government next month.

questions.explanation: Simple future active 'will + V1' becomes passive 'will + be + V3'. Option B wrongly applies future continuous passive ('will be being'), which is not standard for a simple future. Option C uses future perfect passive ('will have been'), implying prior completion — not intended here. Option D uses simple present passive, ignoring the future tense signal entirely.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is written in passive voice?

options.option_text: The journalist published an explosive report yesterday.
An old bridge was demolished by the municipal corporation.
The athlete broke three national records in one event.
Children enjoy playing outdoor games in the evening.

questions.explanation: In option B, the subject 'An old bridge' receives the action ('was demolished'), and the doer follows 'by' — the classic passive structure. Options A, C, and D all have subjects performing the action, making them active voice. A common mistake is to confuse a long subject in active voice with passive construction.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive voice transformation of: 'Can the doctor examine the patient right now?'

options.option_text: Can the patient be examined by the doctor right now?
Could the patient be examined by the doctor right now?
The patient can be examined by the doctor right now.
Can the patient examined by the doctor right now?

questions.explanation: For modal interrogative passive, the structure is: Modal + subject + be + V3, preserving the question form and the original modal. 'Can' is retained unchanged — not shifted to 'could' as in option B. Option C correctly uses 'can be examined' but converts the question into a statement, losing the interrogative. Option D omits 'be', making the verb chain grammatically broken.

questions.stem: Which option correctly converts to passive voice: 'Someone must have taken the important files.'?

options.option_text: The important files must be taken by someone.
The important files must have been taken by someone.
The important files have been taken by someone.
The important files must have taken by someone.

questions.explanation: The active sentence uses a perfect modal 'must have + V3'; its passive is: subject + must have been + V3. Option A uses simple modal passive ('must be taken'), stripping the perfect aspect that signals inference about a past event. Option C drops 'must', converting a deduction into a plain statement of fact. Option D omits 'been', breaking the passive participle chain — a frequent error candidates make.

questions.stem: Identify the correct passive voice of: 'The landlord needs to paint the walls before winter.'

options.option_text: The walls needed to be painted by the landlord before winter.
The walls need to be painted by the landlord before winter.
The walls are being painted by the landlord before winter.
The walls need to have been painted by the landlord before winter.

questions.explanation: For 'need + to + V1', the passive form is 'need + to be + V3', preserving tense. Option A shifts tense to past ('needed'), which contradicts the original present-tense sentence. Option C replaces the infinitive construction with present continuous passive, distorting the meaning from obligation to ongoing action. Option D uses a perfect infinitive passive ('to have been painted'), implying prior completion — an aspect not present in the original.

questions.stem: 'The principal awarded Meera the first prize at the ceremony' has two objects. Which passive transformation is CORRECT?

options.option_text: Meera was awarded the first prize at the ceremony by the principal.
The first prize was awarded Meera at the ceremony by the principal.
Meera had been awarded the first prize at the ceremony by the principal.
The first prize is awarded to Meera at the ceremony by the principal.

questions.explanation: When a ditransitive verb like 'award' takes two objects, either may become the passive subject. Using the indirect object ('Meera') as subject: 'Meera was awarded the first prize by the principal' is the grammatically standard form. Option B promotes the direct object but omits the mandatory preposition 'to' — it must be 'awarded to Meera'. Option C incorrectly shifts the tense to past perfect. Option D uses simple present tense, losing the past-tense context entirely.

questions.stem: Which option is the correct passive voice of: 'Someone had been following the suspect for weeks.'?

options.option_text: The suspect was being followed by someone for weeks.
The suspect had been being followed by someone for weeks.
The suspect has been followed by someone for weeks.
The suspect was followed by someone for weeks.

questions.explanation: Past perfect continuous active ('had been + V-ing') converts to past perfect continuous passive: 'had been being + V3'. Option A uses past continuous passive ('was being followed'), losing the perfect aspect that marks an action ongoing before a past reference point. Option C uses present perfect passive, ignoring the past perfect frame entirely. Option D uses simple past passive, collapsing both the perfect and continuous dimensions — the most tempting wrong answer because it sounds natural, but it fundamentally changes the grammatical meaning.
